planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in humus-rich, moisture-retentive soil in partial to full shade; this woodland species resents hot, dry conditions and performs best with cool root shade through summer.

directions: Geranium reflexum is a woodland cranesbill native to mountain forests of Italy and the western Balkans, closely allied to the mourning widow geranium (G. phaeum) but generally more compact and softly hairy throughout the foliage and stems. Its common name refers to the nodding, reflexed flowers, which open in dusky violet-purple tones and hang downward on wiry stalks held above mounds of deeply lobed, matte green leaves in late spring and early summer. Like its phaeum relatives, it is one of the more reliably shade-tolerant hardy geraniums, coping with the low light and leaf litter of a deciduous woodland floor far better than sun-loving cranesbill species. Established clumps slowly increase and can be divided every few years in spring or immediately after flowering to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or fall in humus-rich, reliably moist soil in partial to full shade; this Balkan woodland species is slower to bulk up than G. phaeum but thrives under the same conditions.

directions: Geranium aristatum hails from the Illyrian Peninsula of the western Balkans, where it grows in deciduous mountain woodland as part of the same phaeum alliance of nodding, reflexed-petaled cranesbills. Its species name refers to the fine bristle-tipped teeth along the leaf margins, a small but distinctive feature that helps separate it from close relatives in the group. In late spring it produces loose clusters of pale pinkish-lilac flowers with darker purple veining and sharply reflexed petals, carried on slender stems above softly lobed foliage. Though still uncommon in cultivation outside specialist collections, it adapts readily to the humus-rich, shaded woodland conditions found in most temperate gardens and can be increased by division of established clumps in spring.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in ordinary, well-drained garden soil in partial shade; it tolerates drier conditions than most woodland geraniums once established and self-sows readily.

directions: Geranium asphodeloides is native to open woodland, scrub, and rocky slopes across the eastern Mediterranean, the Caucasus, and Turkey, where it has adapted to a drier, more seasonal climate than most shade-garden cranesbills. It forms a low, sprawling mound of deeply cut, semi-evergreen leaves on wiry stems, with small, pale pink to near-white flowers whose narrow, notched petals give the blooms a starry, fringed look through a long succession from late spring into summer. Its drought tolerance once rooted in makes it a useful choice for the lightly shaded, drier margins of a woodland garden where more moisture-demanding geraniums falter, and it seeds itself modestly to form a loose colony over time. Established plants are easily lifted and divided in spring to propagate or to curb self-sown spread.
